resilience

/rez-IL-yens/ — stress on IL, rhymes with brilliance · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Resilience is the ability to recover quickly from setbacks and come back strong after being knocked down.

The town's resilience showed as shops reopened days after the storm.

Worked Example

After losing her violin scholarship, Maya enrolled in a community music program and practiced for six months until she earned it back.

Resilience is more precise than 'strength' because it emphasizes the ability to recover from setbacks, not just raw power. Maya didn't just need strength; she needed the capacity to bounce back after being knocked down—that's resilience.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

strength: Strength is the raw power to hold up under pressure or hardship - strong arms, a strong will, a strong bridge. Resilience is more specific: not the power to resist a blow, but the ability to take one, recover, and come back as good as before.

perseverance: Perseverance means steadily continuing on, day after day, despite difficulty - it is about not stopping. Resilience is about what happens after a real setback: being knocked down and springing back. You show perseverance by never quitting; you show resilience by recovering when something knocks you flat.

durability: Durability is the ability of a thing to last through long, hard use - a quality of boots, tools, and bridges that simply do not wear out. Resilience belongs to people and communities as much as things, and it centers on bouncing back after damage, not merely enduring.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

fragility: the tendency to break or fail easily

brittleness: hardness that shatters instead of bending back

Where it sits · how well it holds up under blows — fragility → stability → resilience → invulnerability

fragility vs. resilience: Fragility is the very opposite of resilience: a fragile thing breaks at the first blow, while resilience means springing back after every blow.

stability vs. resilience: Stability is weaker than resilience — a stable thing simply holds steady, but resilience adds the power to recover even after being knocked down.

invulnerability vs. resilience: Invulnerability is stronger than resilience: resilience means bouncing back from harm, while invulnerability means never being harmed in the first place.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — re-

Prefix — re-: back (Latin)

Root — sili

Root — sili: to leap, spring (from salire) (Latin)

Suffix — -ence

Suffix — -ence: state or quality of (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Resilience builds re- ('back') onto the Latin root salire ('to leap, spring') plus -ence ('state or quality'): resilience is literally the quality of leaping back — recovering quickly after being bent, stretched, or knocked down.

Use the root in a new word: somersault

Use the root in a new word: somersault: In a somersault, a gymnast leaps and springs head over heels — the same Latin root salire, 'to leap,' that gives resilience its power to spring back from setbacks.

Word Choice

formal / technical

Resilience names a crucial strength: not just surviving hardship but bouncing back from it. Use it when describing how someone or something recovers from setback or functions well under ongoing pressure. For simple toughness, 'strength' or 'durability' works better.
